title: Metacognitive Awareness and EFL Learners' Perceptions and Experiences in Utilising ChatGPT for Writing Feedback
extended_summary:
This paper examines how EFL learners perceive and experience using ChatGPT for writing feedback, with particular attention to the role of metacognitive awareness. The study asks three main questions: how ChatGPT influences students’ writing experiences and metacognitive awareness, how levels of metacognitive awareness relate to perceptions and practices of ChatGPT use, and what factors shape effective use of ChatGPT for writing feedback.

The intervention took place in a semester-long practical writing course in which one class used AI tools including Poe as an access point to ChatGPT during writing tasks, while another class followed a teacher-led, peer-collaboration approach without AI. The study used a mixed-methods design combining questionnaires, pre/post comparisons, regression analyses, and semi-structured interviews. Outcomes focused on self-reported writing motivation, engagement, self-efficacy, collaborative writing tendency, and metacognitive awareness dimensions such as declarative, procedural, and conditional knowledge, planning, monitoring, and evaluation.

Participants were 40 EFL undergraduates in two English Practical Writing classes at the same institution in Macau, SAR, China. Students were described as mainly from Macau, with Cantonese as a first language for most and some Mandarin speakers from mainland China, and their English proficiency was low to intermediate. Ten students from the AI group also participated in interviews, split between higher and lower metacognitive awareness.

The main findings were that the AI-using group showed significantly higher post-test scores on most self-reported writing and metacognitive outcomes than the non-AI group. Regression and interview findings suggested that metacognitive awareness was strongly associated with more productive use of ChatGPT. Students with higher metacognitive awareness described using ChatGPT more critically and strategically, whereas lower-awareness students were more likely to copy output or struggle to obtain useful feedback. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can support EFL writing development, but its effective use depends heavily on learners’ metacognitive awareness, critical thinking, and cognitive effort.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-method comparative study with a small sample (n=40) in higher education, using two intact classes and quantitative plus interview data. It is not a K-12 study, not a randomized controlled trial at the student level, and reports no standardized effect sizes or confidence intervals, so it fits correlational/quasi-experimental evidence with notable limitations.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported post-test and gain-score differences are consistently positive across motivation, engagement, collaboration, and metacognitive outcomes, with several statistically significant group differences suggesting modest practical impact. However, effect sizes are not reported and the sample is small and non-K-12, so impact is better characterized as modest rather than clearly medium/large.

interventions.use_case: EFL university writing course using Poe/ChatGPT as a writing feedback and revision aid for students to seek comments on their writing, compare suggestions, and support editing/revision during class.
Generative AI used specifically as machine-generated feedback on student writing, contrasted with a non-AI teacher-led and peer-collaboration writing approach.

finding.finding_summary: Across a 15-week writing course, the AI group (n=20) showed significantly higher post-test writing-related outcomes than the non-AI group (n=20), including self-efficacy for writing and other writing experience indicators. Post-test self-efficacy for writing was 3.96 (SD=0.52) in the AI group versus 3.66 (SD=0.34) in the non-AI group (p=0.037), although gain-score differences for self-efficacy were only marginal in the Mann-Whitney test (p=0.064), suggesting literacy-related benefits but with some inconsistency across writing submeasures.
finding.measure: Writing-related questionnaire outcomes in an EFL writing course, especially self-efficacy for writing as part of writing experiences/perceptions
finding.std_deviation: AI post SEW SD=0.52; non-AI post SEW SD=0.34

finding.finding_summary: The AI-supported writing group (n=20) reported significantly stronger motivation, engagement, and collaborative writing tendency than the comparison group (n=20) after the semester-long course. Post-test means favored AI for motivation for writing (4.34 vs 3.59, p<0.001), collaborative writing tendency (4.14 vs 3.58, p<0.001), and writing engagement (4.26 vs 3.48, p<0.001); gain-score tests also favored AI for motivation, collaboration, and engagement (all p<=0.0024, except self-efficacy marginal at p=0.064).
finding.measure: Questionnaire scales for motivation for writing, writing engagement, collaborative writing tendency, and self-efficacy for writing
finding.std_deviation: Motivation post SDs: 0.38 vs 0.35; collaboration post SDs: 0.45 vs 0.37; engagement post SDs: 0.54 vs 0.39

finding.finding_summary: The study found substantial positive effects of AI-supported writing on metacognitive awareness dimensions. Relative to the non-AI group (n=20), the AI group (n=20) scored higher at post-test on declarative knowledge (4.40 vs 3.46), procedural knowledge (4.09 vs 3.54), conditional knowledge (4.26 vs 3.44), planning (4.14 vs 3.64), monitoring (3.97 vs 3.40), and evaluating (4.22 vs 3.50), all p<0.001; regression further showed metacognitive awareness strongly predicted perceptions/experiences of ChatGPT use (b=1.2398, p<0.001, model R²=0.8631).
finding.measure: Metacognitive Writing Strategies Questionnaire dimensions: declarative, procedural, conditional knowledge; planning, monitoring, evaluating; plus regression of metacognitive awareness on ChatGPT-related perceptions/practices
finding.std_deviation: Representative post SDs—DK: 0.27 vs 0.32; PK: 0.47 vs 0.38; CK: 0.36 vs 0.36; Planning: 0.31 vs 0.27; Monitoring: 0.28 vs 0.19; Evaluating: 0.22 vs 0.18
